clue.text: Send in a column, keeping this for the record?

blocks.note: first meaning: what a journalist does when submitting the text of an article
second meaning: a duplicate document retained in the files

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads like advice on archiving a newspaper piece; the phrase is a journalist's verb and also an office noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Reporters 'file' their 'copy' (written text) to the paper, and a duplicate kept in the office archive is also called this.

clue.text: When play opens see trees close together across edge of curtain

indicators.note: an edge is a boundary, so only a letter at the end of the following word is wanted
one piece lies across, i.e. spans and encloses, the other

blocks.note: a common kind of conifer, in the plural
packed close, with no gaps
the final letter of curtain

explanation.surface: A theatregoer watches trees on a painted set crowding in as the curtain goes up on the opening performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Edge' could be either end; here it is the curtain's final letter, slotted in just after the first letter of the word for close together.
explanation.definitionFit: The premiere is the first evening a production is performed, i.e. the occasion when a play opens.

clue.text: Decisive check that may produce basic result?

blocks.note: first meaning: a single test whose outcome settles a question
second meaning: the chemistry paper turns blue in an alkaline (basic) solution

explanation.walkthrough: 'Basic' looks like 'simple', but in chemistry a base is an alkali, which this paper detects.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for a conclusive criterion, borrowed from the chemistry paper that shows acid or alkali.

clue.text: "Charlie," to his younger brother, is cocaine

indicators.note: 'to' here means set next to, so one piece is placed right beside the other

blocks.note: Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet
King Charles's younger brother is Prince Andrew, known as Andy

explanation.surface: A family member reveals what Charlie is nicknamed by his kid brother: cocaine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charlie' is itself slang for cocaine, which tempts a solver to read it as the definition; here it is just the letter C, and the brother is the royal one.
explanation.definitionFit: Candy, as in 'nose candy', is slang for the drug.

clue.text: Sort of dish rebellious group, becoming fossils

blocks.note: a Petri dish is a shallow lab dish for cultures
a dissenting group within a larger body

explanation.surface: A lab dish of cultures has a breakaway colony that is turning to stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Petrifaction is the process by which organic matter turns to stone, the way remains are fossilised.

clue.text: Moved suddenly – small accident

blocks.note: standard abbreviation for small
a prang is British slang for a minor crash, usually in a car

explanation.surface: A driver jerked forward when a minor collision happened.
explanation.definitionFit: Sprang is the past tense of spring, to leap or jump up abruptly.

clue.text: Sharp emotion as glutton tours old French city

indicators.note: to tour is to go all around, so one piece circles another

blocks.note: a greedy eater is called a pig
O is a standard abbreviation for old
Nancy is a city in Lorraine

explanation.surface: A greedy traveller feels a pang on visiting an ancient city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' qualifies nothing in the answer: it is just the letter going inside the glutton, and Nancy is a living city in Lorraine.
explanation.definitionFit: Poignancy is the quality of causing keen sadness or pity, a piercing feeling.

clue.text: Some expressing a sigh of relief

indicators.note: to express is to put into spoken words, so we go by pronunciation

blocks.note: 'phew' is the exclamation of relief

explanation.surface: A few people let out a sigh when the danger passes.
explanation.definitionFit: A small number of things is 'some'; both are vague quantifiers.

clue.text: Tough character to pull up stallion at the start

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading the word from bottom to top, backwards
only the opening letter of the preceding word is kept

blocks.note: to tug is to pull hard
the first letter of stallion

explanation.surface: A horse handler hauls back a stallion right from the start, showing grit.
explanation.definitionFit: Guts means courage or toughness of spirit, the quality of a hardy character.

clue.text: Ceremonial procedure by enthusiast, nothing held back

blocks.note: a ritual act
a fan, as in 'health nut'
zero, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A ceremony put on by a devotee that is kept completely in check.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an Italian musical direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Ritenuto is the score marking telling players to slow down at once, literally 'held back' in Italian.

clue.text: Take off before temperature plunges

indicators.note: says that one piece sits ahead of another in the answer, here the plunging word ahead of the temperature

blocks.note: dives as in drops headlong
standard abbreviation for temperature

explanation.surface: Strip off your layers before the thermometer drops.
explanation.definitionFit: To divest is to remove clothing or strip something away, the same as taking it off.

clue.text: Gay piece has garbage prose needing a rewrite

indicators.note: a rewrite reworks the words, so the letters are put into a new order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic sniffs that a cheerful work is written in rubbish prose and needs redrafting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gay' is John Gay, the 18th-century playwright, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beggar's Opera (1728) is John Gay's ballad opera, so it is a work by him.

clue.text: Without source's origin, do hack job on duchy instead of historian

indicators.note: an origin is a beginning, so the opening letter of source is the one to remove
a hack job is a crude reworking, so the letters are chopped and rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then its S is removed

explanation.surface: An editor, lacking original sources, botches an account of a duchy rather than consulting a historian.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the S (source's first letter) out of INSTEAD, then rearrange DUCHY + INTEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: Thucydidean is the adjective for Thucydides, the ancient Greek chronicler of the Peloponnesian War.

clue.text: Saying hello to adder in August perhaps

indicators.note: saying something means voicing it, so we want a word with the same pronunciation

blocks.note: HI is a greeting
one who adds up, who sums

explanation.surface: Someone greets a snake during a warm month.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adder' looks like the snake, which fits August heat, but it is one who adds.
explanation.definitionFit: August is an example of the hottest part of the year, the height of that season.

clue.text: Impossibility: tin thrown up seen flying down to earth

indicators.note: in a down entry, thrown upward means read from bottom to top, backwards
things sent flying land scattered, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: a no-no is something that is not allowed
Sn is the chemical symbol for tin
taken as written

explanation.surface: A can tossed into the air is seen tumbling back down to the ground; impossible!
explanation.definitionFit: No-nonsense describes a practical, sensible person, which is what being down to earth means.

clue.text: Fibre obtained from mistletoe

indicators.note: the letters are extracted from inside the next word

blocks.note: the run of letters inside the word

explanation.surface: A strand is taken from a sprig of the Christmas plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Istle is a coarse plant fibre from Mexican agave and yucca, used for cord and brushes.

clue.text: Found herbalists' missing recipe, fancy!

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so a letter is dropped
fancy as in elaborate or fanciful, so the letters are freely rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for recipe, as on prescriptions

explanation.surface: Someone discovers that the herb doctors have lost a prescription, and is amazed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' looks like the past tense of find, but it is the verb to set up. Remove R from HERBALISTS and rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To found a company or school is to establish it, to bring it into being.

clue.text: One American rubbishes ignorant English

indicators.note: to rubbish something is to trash it, wrecking its order

blocks.note: taken as written
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A Yank pours scorn on uninformed Brits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'American' here covers all the Americas, including South America.
explanation.definitionFit: An Argentino is a native of Argentina, an inhabitant of the American continent.

clue.text: Chap has one potato he is about to lose?

blocks.note: a man, referred to as 'he'
the contraction 's, as in he's
Roman numeral one
an informal word for a potato

explanation.surface: A fellow clutching a spud seems about to come off second best.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to the proverb 'he who hesitates is lost'.
explanation.definitionFit: By the proverb, someone who dithers is lost, so a person who hesitates is cryptically one about to lose.

clue.text: Barbarian cut grass back, round and round

indicators.note: going back means the word is read in the opposite direction

blocks.note: grass mown and dried
each round shape is an O

explanation.surface: A savage mows the lawn, then circles it again and again.
explanation.walkthrough: HAY reversed gives YAH, then OO.
explanation.definitionFit: A yahoo is a coarse, uncivilised person, from Swift's brutish creatures in Gulliver's Travels.

clue.text: Devotional work, one we possess, read aloud

indicators.note: what is read out loud is judged by its sound, not its spelling

blocks.note: 'one' is a work, i.e. a book, that belongs to us

explanation.surface: A prayer book that we own is recited.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One' refers back to the work in the definition: a book that is ours.
explanation.definitionFit: A Book of Hours is a medieval prayer book arranged by the canonical hours of the day.

clue.text: Cover-up involves some consecutive letters, then some more

blocks.note: three letters next to each other in the alphabet
two further consecutive letters, the start of the alphabet

explanation.surface: A cover-up story about runs of letters in a code, one after another.
explanation.definitionFit: A hijab is a headscarf worn by many Muslim women, a garment that covers the hair.

clue.text: Country cousin initially tricked

indicators.note: initially means at the beginning, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: the first letter of cousin
to have someone is to fool them, as in 'you've been had'

explanation.surface: A rural relative was fooled at the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country cousin' reads as a phrase, but 'Country' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Chad is a nation in north-central Africa.

clue.text: Shout of encouragement for thug

blocks.note: first meaning, as two words: a cry urging someone to continue
second meaning, as one word: a hired heavy

explanation.walkthrough: The same letters split as two words give the cheer and joined as one give the brute.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Go on!' urges someone forward, and a goon is a violent hired enforcer.

clue.text: Crow adopted by some youths

blocks.note: first meaning: the hooded crow, a grey-and-black bird
second meaning: a hooded sweatshirt, worn by many teenagers

explanation.walkthrough: 'Crow' looks like a verb (to boast) but is the bird; 'adopted' means taken up as clothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is a colloquial word both for the hooded crow and for the hooded top favoured by young people.

clue.text: Predict judge is to recall celebrity would-be Slough bomber

indicators.note: recall means call back, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: to bet on an outcome is to forecast it
J is the abbreviation for judge
a big name is a famous person

explanation.surface: A judge is asked to forecast and remember a famous would-be terrorist.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is an English town west of London; Sir John Betjeman's poem 'Slough' begins 'Come, friendly bombs, and fall on Slough!'
explanation.definitionFit: The poet laureate wished bombs on the town in verse, making him a would-be bomber only in jest.

clue.text: An inflatable horse, dirty-looking all round

indicators.note: going all the way round means one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: drab and grimy
horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H

explanation.surface: A grimy blow-up horse, the kind of pool toy left out all summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse' looks like the animal toy, but it is drug slang for heroin, H, which goes inside DINGY.
explanation.definitionFit: A dinghy is a small boat, and many are rubber ones blown up with air.

clue.text: Rally postmen, everyone having lost heart

indicators.note: losing its heart leaves a word with only its outside letters

blocks.note: split as post + men: a jamb is the upright post of a door frame, and OR is 'other ranks', soldiers below officer level
just the outside letters of everyone

explanation.surface: Mail carriers gather, but morale has drained from all of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Postmen' splits into post + men.
explanation.definitionFit: A jamboree is a large gathering, especially of Scouts, so a rally or celebration.
